title: Argumenter
intro: Raconte des enquêtes au passé, rapporte ce que les autres ont dit, défends tes idées avec les bons connecteurs et parle comme un vrai anglophone avec make, do et compagnie.

boss.name: Le Reporter
boss.taunt: Une seule question : sauras-tu rapporter mes paroles sans la moindre erreur ? J'en doute… et je vais l'écrire en première page !
boss.defeat: Arrêtez les presses ! Gros titre de demain : « Le Reporter battu à plate couture ».

units.title: Le passé du passé
units.goal: Raconter une histoire au passé en montrant ce qui était arrivé avant, avec le past perfect.

lesson.text: Dans une histoire au passé, tu dois parfois remonter **encore plus loin** : ce qui s'était passé AVANT. Pour ça, l'anglais utilise le **past perfect**, l'équivalent de notre plus-que-parfait (« j'avais mangé », « elle était partie »).

lesson.title: Le past perfect
lesson.text: [[had]] + participe passé, **pareil pour toutes les personnes** : [[I had finished]], [[she had left]], [[they had gone]]. Négation : [[hadn't]]. Question : [[Had you seen him before?]] Contraction : [[I'd]], [[she'd]]… mais attention, [['d]] peut aussi vouloir dire [[would]] ! Révise les participes : [[steal]] → [[stole]] → [[stolen]], [[hide]] → [[hid]] → [[hidden]], [[run]] → [[ran]] → [[run]].

head: Phrase
Ce qui s'est passé
rows: J'arrive, **puis** le bus part : je le vois partir.
[[When I arrived, the bus had left.]]
Le bus part **d'abord** : quand j'arrive, il n'est plus là.
[[By the time we got there, the cake had disappeared.]]
[[It was the first time I had seen a moose.]]
Après [[It was the first time]], on met le past perfect.

lesson.title: Le past perfect continuous
lesson.text: [[had been]] + verbe en **-ing** : une action qui **durait** jusqu'à un moment du passé. [[She had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally came.]] = Elle attendait **depuis** une heure quand l'autobus est enfin arrivé. Avec les verbes d'état ([[know]], [[like]], [[want]]…), pas de -ing : [[We had known each other for years.]]

items.en: By the time the police arrived, the thief had already left.
items.fr: Le temps que la police arrive, le voleur était déjà parti.

items.en: I realized that I had left my keys at school.
items.fr: Je me suis rendu compte que j'avais oublié mes clés à l'école.

items.en: Had you ever seen the suspect before that night?
items.fr: Avais-tu déjà vu le suspect avant cette nuit-là ?

items.en: They had been investigating the case for months.
items.fr: Ils enquêtaient sur l'affaire depuis des mois.

items.en: The ground was wet because it had been raining all night.
items.fr: Le sol était mouillé parce qu'il avait plu toute la nuit.

lesson.text: Piège de francophone : « Il attendait **depuis** deux heures » ne se dit **jamais** [[He was waiting since two hours]]. On dit [[He had been waiting for two hours]]. Durée → [[for]] ; point de départ → [[since]] ([[since noon]]).
Ne mets pas le past perfect partout ! Si tu racontes les actions **dans l'ordre**, le past simple suffit : [[I opened the door and saw a footprint.]] Le past perfect sert à **revenir en arrière**.

lines.en: Ethan, you were the first person in the gym this morning, right?
lines.fr: Ethan, tu étais la première personne dans le gymnase ce matin, c'est ça ?

lines.en: Yes, but when I got there, someone had already taken the cake.

lines.en: Small footprints with chocolate on them. Someone had been eating the cake on the stairs!
lines.fr: Des petites empreintes de pas pleines de chocolat. Quelqu'un avait mangé le gâteau dans l'escalier !

lines.en: Chocolate footprints? That's our best clue. Let's follow them!
lines.fr: Des empreintes au chocolat ? C'est notre meilleur indice. Suivons-les !

lesson.text: Le sais-tu ? Sherlock Holmes, le détective le plus célèbre du monde, a été inventé par l'écrivain écossais Arthur Conan Doyle à la fin du dix-neuvième siècle.

grammar.q: When we got to the theatre, the movie ___, so we missed the beginning.
grammar.explain: Le film a commencé AVANT notre arrivée : past perfect, had + participe passé.

grammar.q: She ___ for two hours when her mom finally called.
grammar.explain: « Elle attendait depuis deux heures » à un moment du passé : had been + -ing, avec for.

grammar.q: By the time I woke up, my brother ___ all the pancakes.
grammar.explain: By the time + passé → l'autre action était déjà finie : had eaten.

grammar.q: Quelle phrase veut dire que le bus était déjà parti quand je suis arrivé ?
choices: When I arrived, the bus left.
When I arrived, the bus had left.
When I arrived, the bus was leaving.
When I arrived, the bus leaves.
grammar.explain: Had left = le bus est parti avant mon arrivée. Left tout seul = il part juste après.

grammar.q: ___ you ever met her before the party?
grammar.explain: « Avant la fête » est un moment passé : on remonte plus loin avec had + participe (met).

grammar.q: Quel est le participe passé de steal ?
grammar.explain: steal → stole → stolen : Someone had stolen my bike.

grammar.q: By the time we reached the station, the train ___.
grammar.explain: Le train est parti avant notre arrivée : had left.

grammar.q: Liam was exhausted because he ___ all afternoon.
grammar.explain: Une action qui a duré avant un moment du passé : had been + -ing.

grammar.q: It was the first time I ___ a real moose.
grammar.explain: Après It was the first time, on utilise le past perfect : had seen.

grammar.q: ___ she already gone home when you called?
grammar.explain: Question au past perfect : Had + sujet + participe passé.

grammar.q: By the time she was ten, Maya ___ in four different cities.
grammar.explain: Avant ses dix ans, c'était déjà fait : had lived.

grammar.q: When I opened the fridge, I realized that someone ___ my sandwich.
grammar.explain: Quelqu'un l'a mangé AVANT que j'ouvre le frigo : had eaten.

grammar.q: The ground was wet because it ___ all night.
grammar.explain: La pluie a duré toute la nuit avant ce moment : had been raining.

grammar.q: When I got home, my sister has already eaten dinner.
grammar.explain: L'histoire est au passé (got) : on remonte avec had, pas has.

grammar.q: They had been waiting since two hours when the door finally opened.
grammar.explain: Une durée (two hours) → for. Since s'emploie avec un point de départ.

grammar.q: I had never saw such a strange footprint before.
grammar.explain: Après had, il faut le participe passé : seen, pas saw.

grammar.q: By the time the police arrived, the thief had already ran away.
grammar.explain: run → ran → run : après had, c'est le participe run.

grammar.q: Had you finish your homework before the movie started?
grammar.explain: Had + participe passé : finished.

reading.title: The Case of the Missing Medal
reading.text:
On the morning of the big swim meet, Malik opened his locker and froze. His gold medal was missing. He had brought it to the pool the day before to show his teammates, and he was sure that he had locked the door before he left.

Malik decided to investigate. He looked for clues and soon noticed a small wet footprint near the lockers. It was much too small to be his. Then he spoke to the only witness, the caretaker, Gilles. Gilles had been cleaning the hallway all evening, and he hadn't seen any suspects. However, he remembered hearing quick footsteps and a little laugh just before closing time.

Malik thought about it. Who had small feet, had been at the pool that evening, and loved to laugh? Suddenly, he realized what had happened. His little sister, Zoé, had come with their dad to pick him up after practice. While Malik was in the shower, she had found the locker key in his jacket.

Malik called home right away. His dad answered and started to laugh. Zoé had been wearing the medal since breakfast and pretending to be an Olympic champion. She wasn't really guilty of anything bad. She had only wanted to feel like her big brother for a day.

That afternoon, Malik swam faster than ever and won a second medal. When he got home, he gave it to Zoé. The case was solved, and everybody was happy.

questions.q: Why did Malik think that the footprint wasn't his?
What had Gilles been doing all evening?
How had Zoé opened the locker?
choices: She had asked Gilles for help.
The locker had been unlocked all night.
She had used the key from Malik's jacket.

questions.q: Why did Malik suspect his sister?
choices: Gilles had seen her take the medal.
The clues matched her: small feet, a laugh, and being at the pool.
She had told him about her plan.
She had won a medal the year before.

questions.q: What kind of person is Zoé, probably?
choices: A playful little sister who admires her brother
A shy girl who never laughs

questions.q: How did the story end?
choices: Malik won another medal and gave it to his sister.
Zoé gave the medal to Gilles.

units.title: Il a dit que…
units.goal: Rapporter ce que quelqu'un a dit, demandé ou ordonné, avec les bons temps et les bons verbes.

lesson.text: Pour rapporter les paroles de quelqu'un, on utilise le **discours indirect** (reported speech). Quand le verbe d'introduction est au passé ([[said]], [[told]], [[asked]]), on fait souvent **reculer les temps d'un cran** : c'est le **backshift**.

head: Paroles exactes
Discours rapporté
rows: [[She said she had lost her phone.]]

lesson.title: Say ou tell ?
lesson.text: [[say]] + ce qui est dit : [[She said that she was hungry.]] [[tell]] + **la personne** : [[She told me that she was hungry.]] On ne dit **jamais** [[He said me]] ! ([[He said to me]] est possible, mais plus rare.) Le [[that]] est facultatif : [[She told me she was hungry.]]

lesson.title: Les questions rapportées
lesson.text: Dans une question rapportée, **plus d'inversion**, plus de [[do]]/[[did]], plus de point d'interrogation : sujet + verbe. [[Where do you live?]] → [[She asked me where I lived.]] Question oui/non → [[if]] ou [[whether]] : [[Are you ready?]] → [[He asked if I was ready.]]

lesson.title: Ordres, demandes et verbes rapporteurs
lesson.text: Ordre : [[told me to]] + verbe ; interdiction : [[told me not to]] + verbe ; demande : [[asked me to]]. Autres verbes : [[admit]] et [[deny]] + -ing ([[He denied breaking the vase.]]) ; [[warn someone not to]] ; [[remind someone to]] ; [[refuse to]] ; [[insist on]] + -ing ; [[apologize for]] + -ing ; [[complain that]] ; [[suggest]] + -ing ([[She suggested going to the park.]]) — jamais [[suggest me to]] !

head: Dans les paroles
Dans le récit

items.en: The coach told us not to skate near the river.
items.fr: L'entraîneur nous a dit de ne pas patiner près de la rivière.

items.en: My mom asked me where I had put her keys.

items.en: She asked me whether I was coming to the game.

lesson.text: Piège n° 1 : [[She asked me where did I live]] ✗ → [[She asked me where I lived]] ✓. Piège n° 2 : le backshift n'est **pas obligatoire** si c'est encore vrai ([[He said Ottawa is the capital of Canada]]) ou si le verbe d'introduction est au présent ([[She says she is tired]]). Dans les exercices, quand l'histoire est finie (« hier », « le mois dernier », « ce soir-là »), on recule les temps.

grammar.q: He asked me where ___.
grammar.explain: Question rapportée : pas d'inversion, pas de did. Sujet + verbe : where I lived.

grammar.q: Last month, Lucas said: "I will help you tomorrow." → Last month, Lucas said that he would help me ___.
grammar.explain: La scène est passée depuis longtemps : tomorrow devient the next day (ou the following day).

grammar.q: Last week, Ana said that she ___ come to my party that night.

grammar.q: Last Monday, Noah said: "I have finished my project." → Noah told me that he ___ his project.

grammar.q: My parents told me ___ my phone at the dinner table.
grammar.explain: Interdiction rapportée : told me not to + verbe.

grammar.q: Sofia said that she had seen the movie ___.
grammar.explain: Yesterday devient the day before (ou the previous day) dans un récit.

grammar.q: He refused ___ me his password.
grammar.explain: Refuse + to + verbe.

grammar.q: Mom reminded me to taking out the garbage.
grammar.explain: Remind someone to + verbe de base : to take.

reading.title: Interview with a Legend
reading.text:
Last week, Léa interviewed Madame Gagnon, the oldest teacher at her school, for the student newspaper. Madame Gagnon was going to retire at the end of the year, and everybody wanted to know her secrets.

First, Léa asked her how she had become a teacher. Madame Gagnon replied that she had started her career in a tiny village school before she moved to Ottawa. She admitted that she had been terrified on her first day. In fact, she had forgotten all her students' names by lunchtime!

Then Léa asked whether teaching had changed a lot. The teacher pointed out that her students now used tablets instead of chalkboards, but she insisted that kids hadn't really changed. They still laughed at the same jokes, she said, and they still complained about homework.

Léa wondered what her favourite memory was. Madame Gagnon smiled and explained that one winter, her whole class had built a giant snow castle in the schoolyard. The principal had warned them not to make it too high, but they had refused to stop. It had become so big that the town newspaper had published a picture of it.

At the end, Madame Gagnon reminded Léa to study hard, and she suggested that every student should read at least one book a month. She told her that a good book was the best friend you could have.

The next day, Léa wrote her article. It became the most popular article of the year.

questions.q: What did Madame Gagnon admit about her first day?
According to Madame Gagnon, what hasn't really changed?
What had the principal told the class?
choices: Not to make the castle too high
To send a picture to the newspaper
Not to play in the snow

questions.q: What did Madame Gagnon suggest?
choices: That every student should read a book a month
That students should write for the newspaper
That kids should use more tablets
That Léa should become a teacher

questions.q: What does the snow castle story show about Madame Gagnon's class?
choices: They were afraid of the principal.
They were determined and worked well together.

questions.q: Why was the article probably so popular?
choices: Because many students knew and liked Madame Gagnon
Because it had a picture of the principal
Because Léa was the principal's daughter

units.title: Les connecteurs
units.goal: Relier tes idées pour argumenter : opposer, ajouter, donner une conséquence ou un but.

lesson.text: Pour gagner un débat, il ne suffit pas d'avoir de bonnes idées : il faut les **relier**. Les connecteurs servent à opposer ([[although]], [[however]]), à ajouter ([[moreover]]), à donner une conséquence ([[therefore]]) ou un but ([[in order to]], [[so that]]).

lesson.title: Although ou despite ?
lesson.text: [[although]] et [[even though]] + **phrase complète** (sujet + verbe) : [[Although it was raining, we played outside.]] [[despite]] et [[in spite of]] + **nom** ou **-ing** : [[Despite the rain, we played outside.]] [[In spite of being tired, he finished.]] On ne dit **jamais** [[despite of]] !

lesson.title: However, la virgule et le but
lesson.text: [[However]] commence souvent une nouvelle phrase, suivi d'une virgule : [[It was a great movie. However, the ending was sad.]] Pour un but : [[in order to]] + verbe ([[We left early in order to catch the bus.]]) ; [[so that]] + sujet + modal ([[I whispered so that the baby wouldn't wake up.]]). Après un verbe au passé, [[so that]] + [[could]] / [[would]].

items.en: Despite the cold weather, hundreds of people skated on the canal.
items.fr: Malgré le froid, des centaines de personnes ont patiné sur le canal.

items.en: My sister loves winter, whereas I prefer summer.
items.fr: Ma sœur adore l'hiver, alors que moi, je préfère l'été.

items.en: You won't get into the game unless you buy a ticket.
items.fr: Tu n'entreras pas au match à moins d'acheter un billet.

items.en: The roads were icy. As a result, all the buses were cancelled.
items.fr: Les routes étaient glacées. Résultat : tous les autobus ont été annulés.

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : « même si » a deux traductions ! [[even though]] = c'est **vrai** ([[Even though I was tired, I stayed up.]]) ; [[even if]] = c'est une **hypothèse** ([[Even if it rains tomorrow, we'll go.]]). Et [[unless]] contient déjà la négation : [[unless you don't hurry]] ✗ → [[unless you hurry]] ✓.

lines.en: I think we should ban phones at school. They're a huge distraction.
lines.fr: Je pense qu'on devrait interdire les téléphones à l'école. Ils nous distraient énormément.

lines.en: I see your point. However, phones can be useful for research.
lines.fr: Je comprends ton point de vue. Cependant, les téléphones peuvent être utiles pour faire de la recherche.

lines.en: True, but students often play games in class even though it's against the rules.
lines.fr: C'est vrai, mais les élèves jouent souvent à des jeux en classe, même si c'est interdit.

lines.en: On the other hand, some students need their phones in order to contact their parents.
lines.fr: D'un autre côté, certains élèves ont besoin de leur téléphone afin de joindre leurs parents.

lines.en: Okay, phones could stay in lockers so that students can use them at lunch.
lines.fr: D'accord, les téléphones pourraient rester dans les casiers pour que les élèves puissent s'en servir au dîner.

lines.en: That sounds fair. Despite our different points of view, I think we've found a solution!
lines.fr: Ça me semble juste. Malgré nos points de vue différents, je pense qu'on a trouvé une solution !

reading.title: Should School Start Later?
reading.text:
Should our school day start an hour later? Last week, our class held a debate on this question, and the room was divided.

Priya's team argued in favour of a later start. Although most students go to bed at a reasonable time, many of them still feel exhausted in the morning. Teenagers' bodies naturally want to fall asleep later than adults' bodies, so getting up at six o'clock is a real struggle. Moreover, tired students find it hard to pay attention. As a result, the first class of the day is often the least productive. A later start would therefore help everyone learn better.

Samuel's team disagreed. They pointed out that a later start would also mean a later finish. Students who play sports or take music lessons would have less time in the afternoon. Some parents, on the other hand, drop their kids off on their way to work, and a later start might cause them serious problems. Samuel also argued that, unless students put their phones away at night, an extra hour of sleep would change nothing.

In the end, the class voted. Despite Samuel's strong arguments, Priya's team won by just a few votes. However, everyone agreed on one thing: both sides had made fair points. Our teacher suggested writing a letter to the principal in order to share our ideas, so that the whole school could discuss them.

Whether the school will change its schedule is still a mystery. But one thing is sure: we have never disagreed so politely!

units.title: Make, do et compagnie
units.goal: Utiliser les bonnes associations de mots avec make, do, take, have, pay, keep, catch, break, save et waste.

lesson.text: En anglais, certains verbes « vont » avec certains noms : ce sont des **collocations**. Le piège : traduire mot à mot. « Faire une erreur » = [[make a mistake]], mais « faire attention » = [[pay attention]] ! La solution : apprendre ces expressions **en bloc**.

lesson.title: Make ou do ?
lesson.text: [[make]] = **créer, fabriquer, produire un résultat** : [[make a cake]], [[make a mistake]], [[make a decision]], [[make noise]], [[make friends]], [[make money]], [[make an effort]], [[make progress]], [[make your bed]]. [[do]] = **activités, tâches, travail** : [[do homework]], [[do the dishes]], [[do the laundry]], [[do research]], [[do your best]], [[do someone a favour]], [[do well]].

head: Verbe
Collocations
rows: a picture, a break, a test, your time, a shower, notes
fun, a party, a good time, lunch, a test
a secret, a promise, calm, in touch
a cold, the bus, a ball
a promise, a record, the rules

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : « faire une photo » → [[take a picture]] ; « faire attention » → [[pay attention]] ; « faire une fête » → [[have a party]] ; « s'amuser » → [[have fun]] ; « faire un effort » → [[make an effort]] ; « battre un record » → [[break a record]] ; « perdre son temps » → [[waste your time]] ; « gagner du temps » → [[save time]]. Et « passer un examen » → [[take a test]] (au Canada, on dit aussi [[write a test]]), car [[pass a test]] veut dire **réussir** l'examen !

lesson.title: Les paires contraires
lesson.text: Certaines collocations vont par deux : [[keep a promise]] (tenir) ↔ [[break a promise]] (ne pas tenir) ; [[save time]] ↔ [[waste time]] ; [[catch the bus]] (attraper) ↔ [[miss the bus]] (rater).

reading.title: Félix's Busy Saturday
reading.text:
On Friday night, Félix made a big decision: this Saturday, he wouldn't waste a single minute. He wrote a long list of things to do, and he promised himself that he would do his best.

First, he made his bed and did the dishes before his parents even woke up. Then he got ready to go to the arena, where he had to take a skating test at nine o'clock. Unfortunately, he hadn't paid attention to the time, and he missed his bus. He ran to the next stop and caught another one just in time. Although he was nervous, he passed the test easily.

In the afternoon, his best friend Amir asked him to do him a favour. Amir's family was having a garage sale and needed help. The two boys made signs, carried boxes and talked to customers. They made a lot of money for the family, had a lot of fun, and took dozens of funny pictures.

By the evening, Félix was exhausted. He had caught a cold in the rain that morning, and his nose was running. Earlier that week, he had promised to play a board game with his little sister, and he didn't want to break his promise. So he made an effort, played two games with her, and even let her win.

Before he fell asleep, Félix looked at his list. Every item had a check mark next to it. "What a waste of a Saturday," he joked to his mom. She laughed. "You didn't waste a second!"

units.title: Poser autrement
units.goal: Poser des questions polies et indirectes, et raconter plus élégamment avec les propositions participiales.

lesson.text: Deux façons de **poser autrement** : les **questions indirectes**, pour demander poliment (à un inconnu dans la rue, à la réception d'un hôtel, à ta patronne), et les **propositions participiales**, pour raconter de façon plus compacte et plus élégante. Les deux rapportent des points à l'examen Cambridge !

lesson.title: Les questions indirectes
lesson.text: On commence par une formule polie ([[Could you tell me…]], [[Do you know…]], [[Do you happen to know…]], [[I was wondering…]], [[I'd like to know…]]), puis on met le mot interrogatif + **sujet + verbe**, comme dans une phrase normale. **Plus d'inversion, plus de do / does / did** : [[Where is the station?]] → [[Could you tell me where the station is?]] ; [[What time does it open?]] → [[Do you know what time it opens?]] (le **-s** revient !). Question oui/non → [[if]] ou [[whether]] : [[Is it free?]] → [[Do you know if it's free?]] Contrairement au discours rapporté, **pas de recul des temps** : le présent reste au présent. Encore plus poli : [[Would you mind]] + -ing ([[Would you mind telling me…?]]).

head: Question directe
Question indirecte
rows: [[Could you tell me where the washroom is?]]
[[Do you know what time the train leaves?]]
[[Can you tell me how much these tickets cost?]]
[[I'd like to know if the parcel arrived.]]
[[Do you happen to know whether this seat is taken?]]
[[Do you know who broke the window?]]

lesson.text: Piège n° 1 : [[Could you tell me where is the station?]] ✗ → [[where the station is]] ✓. Piège n° 2 : [[Do you know what time does it open?]] ✗ → [[what time it opens]] ✓. Piège n° 3 : la ponctuation suit la **formule de départ** : [[Could you tell me…?]] garde son point d'interrogation, mais [[I wonder where she is.]] et [[I was wondering if you could help me.]] finissent par un **point**. Cas spécial : quand [[who]] ou [[what]] est **le sujet** (qui / qu'est-ce qui), l'ordre ne bouge pas : [[Who called?]] → [[Do you know who called?]]

lesson.title: Les propositions participiales
lesson.text: Elles remplacent une proposition entière par un participe. **1.** Verbe en [[-ing]] : deux actions en même temps, ou une cause : [[Walking home, I saw a moose.]] (= pendant que je marchais) ; [[Feeling sick, she stayed in bed.]] (= comme elle se sentait malade). **2.** [[Having]] + participe passé : une action **terminée avant** l'autre : [[Having finished my homework, I went skating.]] **3.** Participe passé seul : sens **passif** : [[Written in French, the letter was hard for him to read.]] (= comme elle était écrite en français). **4.** Négation : [[Not]] se place **devant** : [[Not knowing what to do, I called my mom.]]

lesson.title: La règle d'or : le même sujet !
lesson.text: Le sujet caché du participe doit être **le sujet de la phrase principale**. [[Walking into the kitchen, I smelled pancakes.]] ✓ (c'est moi qui entre). Mais [[Walking into the kitchen, the smell of pancakes surprised me.]] ✗ : l'odeur entre dans la cuisine ?! Même chose pour [[Having eaten all the cookies, the jar was empty.]] ✗ : le pot a mangé les biscuits ? Dis plutôt : [[Having eaten all the cookies, Liam hid the empty jar.]]

grammar.explain: Le does disparaît, mais le -s de la 3e personne revient : the bus leaves.

grammar.q: ___ my homework, I went outside to play basketball.
grammar.explain: Action terminée avant l'autre : Having + participe passé (finished).

grammar.q: ___ what to do, I called my grandma.
grammar.explain: La négation d'une participiale : Not se place devant le verbe en -ing.

grammar.q: Quelle phrase est correcte ?
choices: Walking into the kitchen, the smell of pancakes surprised me.
Walking into the kitchen, I smelled pancakes.
Walking into the kitchen, the pancakes were ready.
Walking into the kitchen, it smelled of pancakes.
grammar.explain: Le sujet de la principale doit faire l'action du participe : c'est moi qui entre, donc I smelled…

grammar.q: I was wondering ___ you could lend me your bike this weekend.
grammar.explain: Demande oui/non indirecte : I was wondering if (ou whether) + sujet + verbe.

grammar.lead: Where is the lost and found?
grammar.q: Could you tell me where ___?
grammar.explain: Dans une question indirecte, le verbe passe après le sujet : where the lost and found is.

grammar.lead: What time does the pool close?
grammar.q: Do you know what time the pool ___?
grammar.explain: Plus de does dans la question indirecte, donc le -s revient sur le verbe : the pool closes.

grammar.q: I'd like to know ___ the parcel arrived.
grammar.explain: Question oui/non rendue indirecte : if ou whether, et le did disparaît (arrived).

grammar.q: Can I ask you how old ___?
grammar.explain: Sujet + verbe après how old : how old your dog is.

grammar.q: ___ the whole pizza, Liam felt a little sick.
grammar.explain: Il a mangé la pizza AVANT d'être malade : Having + participe passé (eaten).

grammar.q: ___ in a hurry, the email was full of mistakes.
grammar.explain: Le courriel a été écrit (sens passif) : participe passé seul, Written.

grammar.q: ___ the answer, Zoé stayed quiet.
grammar.explain: Comme elle ne savait pas : Not + -ing, avec not devant.

grammar.q: Do you know what time the store open?
grammar.explain: Sans does, le verbe reprend le -s de la 3e personne : the store opens.

grammar.q: I wonder that the library is open today.
grammar.explain: Pour une question oui/non indirecte : if ou whether, jamais that.

grammar.q: Don't knowing anyone at the party, Léa felt shy.
grammar.explain: On nie une participiale avec Not : Not knowing anyone…

grammar.q: Having finish the race, the runners drank lots of water.
grammar.explain: Having + participe passé : Having finished.

grammar.q: In waiting for the bus, I read a whole chapter.
grammar.explain: « En attendant » ne se traduit pas par In waiting : on dit While waiting (ou simplement Waiting).

reading.title: The Most Polite Tourist in Ottawa
reading.text:
Having lived in a small village all his life, Grandpa Samuel had never visited a big city. So when his granddaughter Chloé invited him to Ottawa, he prepared carefully. Not wanting to sound rude, he practised polite questions in English for weeks.

On his first morning, Grandpa went downtown alone. Feeling a little confused by all the traffic, he stopped a passer-by. "Excuse me, could you tell me where the Parliament buildings are?" he asked. The woman smiled and gave him clear directions. Encouraged, he kept going.

At a convenience store, he asked the cashier whether the buses were running on time. At the museum, he wanted to know what time the guided tour started. At a bakery, he even asked the baker if she would mind sharing her recipe for butter tarts. Everyone seemed charmed by his perfect manners.

There was just one problem. Busy chatting with half the city, Grandpa forgot to check the time. When he finally looked at his watch, it was already six o'clock, and Chloé had been waiting for him at home for over an hour.

Exhausted but delighted, he arrived with a box of butter tarts, three maps and a long list of new friends. "I'm so sorry I'm late," he said. "But do you know how many kind people live in this city?"

Chloé laughed. "Grandpa, next time, could you please tell me where you're going before you leave?"

questions.q: Why did Grandpa Samuel practise his English questions before the trip?
choices: Because he had an English exam
Because he didn't want to sound rude
Because Chloé had asked him to
Because he wanted to find a job in Ottawa

questions.q: What did Grandpa want to know at the museum?
choices: Whether the buses were on time
What time the guided tour started

questions.q: Why did Grandpa get home so late?
choices: He had been so busy talking to people that he forgot the time.
He had missed the last bus.
He had got lost near the Rideau Canal.
The museum tour had finished very late.

questions.q: What can we guess about the people Grandpa met?
choices: They were friendly and happy to help him.

questions.q: What is Chloé really asking for at the end?
choices: She wants Grandpa to stop asking questions.
She wants to know how many people live in Ottawa.
She wants him to buy more butter tarts.
She would like him to tell her his plans next time.
